spans.text: In PostgreSQL an UPDATE writes a new version of the row rather than overwriting the old one in place.
Each row version records the id of the transaction that created it in its xmin field.
Under Repeatable Read, a transaction that reads the same row twice sees the same data both times, even if another transaction committed a change to that row in between.
VACUUM reclaims row versions that are no longer visible to any running transaction.
A plain SELECT does not block a concurrent UPDATE of the same row, and a concurrent UPDATE does not block that SELECT.
PostgreSQL's default isolation level is Read Committed.
Under Read Committed, each statement in a transaction sees a snapshot taken at the moment that statement began, so two statements in one transaction can see different data.
Row versions written by a transaction that later rolls back are never visible to other transactions.
PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read is stronger than the SQL standard requires at that level: it also prevents phantom reads, which the standard permits under Repeatable Read.
Under SERIALIZABLE, a transaction that has only run SELECTs can still be aborted with a serialization failure.
Under Repeatable Read, the transaction's snapshot is taken at its first statement that reads or writes data, not at BEGIN.
Under Repeatable Read, a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE that waits on a row updated and committed by another transaction fails with a serialization error instead of returning the newer version.
Two transactions can each commit successfully under Repeatable Read and together leave the database violating a rule that neither of them violated on its own.
A transaction that rolls back after inserting a row still consumes the sequence value it took, so an identity column can contain gaps.
A single long-running transaction can prevent VACUUM from removing dead row versions in tables that transaction never touched.
Under Read Committed, an UPDATE that blocks on a row locked by another transaction will re-evaluate its WHERE clause against the newly committed version of that row once the lock is released.
A row version's xmax field can be set on a row that was never deleted, because xmax also records a transaction that locked or updated the row.
